name: The Gish Gallop
statement: The Gish gallop overwhelms an opponent with a rapid barrage of arguments, regardless of merit, so none can be rebutted in time.
statementAccent: a rapid barrage of arguments, regardless of merit
meaning: The Gish gallop is a rhetorical technique in which a debater fires off an excessive number of arguments, half-truths, and misrepresentations in quick succession, prioritising quantity over accuracy or strength. The sheer volume makes it practically impossible for an opponent to address every point within a debate’s time limits, leaving weak claims unanswered and appearing unrefuted to the audience.
mechanism: It exploits an asymmetry sometimes called Brandolini’s law: refuting a false or sloppy claim takes far more time and effort than making one. Because a rebuttal requires explanation while an assertion requires only a sentence, the galloper can always out-pace the responder, especially when the audience lacks the background to fact-check on the fly.

examples.text: Creationist Duane Gish, in university debates during the 1980s and 1990s, would run through many claims for 45 minutes to an hour, a style Eugenie Scott said produced "torrents of error" opponents had no realistic chance of rebutting in the format.

According to the National Center for Science Education, biologist Kenneth R. Miller used the same rapid-argument technique against Gish during a debate at the University of Arizona on 12 February 1982.
Michael Shermer, who also debated Gish, observed that Gish reused near-identical openings, slides, and jokes across many debates, reinforcing the pre-packaged, hard-to-counter barrage.

whyItMatters: Recognising the Gish gallop helps audiences see that an unanswered claim is not the same as an unrefutable one. It explains why debate "wins" on stage often have little bearing on which side’s claims are actually true, and it justifies pre-empting known arguments rather than trying to answer everything live.
limits: The term is informal and applied retrospectively as a critique rather than a formally defined fallacy, so labelling an opponent’s rapid argumentation a "Gish gallop" can itself dismiss a legitimate multi-point case. Structured formats with pre-submitted arguments limit its effectiveness compared to free-form live debate.
misreadings: Not every fast or multi-pronged argument is a Gish gallop; the term specifically implies disregard for the arguments’ accuracy or strength, not merely their number.
origin: The term was coined in 1994 by anthropologist Eugenie Scott, founding executive director of the National Center for Science Education, who named it after creationist Duane Gish, its "most avid practitioner."

sources.text: Gish gallop, Wikipedia. — Eugenie Scott’s 1994 coinage after Duane Gish and the Brandolini’s-law mechanism.
National Center for Science Education, "NCSE and the Gish Gallop." — Scott’s original description and the 1982 Miller-Gish debate.
